title: Unit 1: My First Day at a New School
content:
Emre is fourteen years old, and last month his family moved from Ankara to Izmir. On his first day at the new school, he felt very nervous because he did not know anyone. His mother drove him to school and told him to smile and be friendly.

In the first lesson, the maths teacher asked Emre to introduce himself to the class. His hands were shaking, but he talked about his hobbies: basketball and drawing comics. After the lesson, a boy called Deniz came to his desk and said that he also loved comics.

At lunch, Deniz invited Emre to sit with his friends in the school garden. They talked about their favourite superheroes and made plans to play basketball after school on Friday. When Emre got home, he told his mother that the day had been much better than he had expected. He was not nervous any more, and he was looking forward to the next day.

title: Unit 2: The Saturday Market
content:
Every Saturday morning, Ayse goes to the open-air market near her home with her grandmother. The market opens at seven o'clock, and the best fruit and vegetables are usually sold before ten. Her grandmother always says that you should never buy tomatoes without smelling them first.

The market is noisy and colourful. Sellers shout the prices of their products, and some of them give free samples of cheese and olives. Ayse's favourite stall belongs to an old man who sells honey from his own bees in the mountains. He has been coming to the market for more than thirty years.

Shopping at the market is cheaper than shopping at the supermarket, but it takes more time. Ayse and her grandmother usually carry two heavy bags home. After that, they make a big breakfast together with fresh bread, eggs, cheese and the honey they bought.

title: Unit 3: Learning to Cook
content:
When Selin started university, she lived alone for the first time. In the first few weeks, she ate fast food almost every day because she did not know how to cook. She soon felt tired and spent too much money, so she decided to learn.

Her first attempt was a simple pasta dish, but she forgot to add salt to the water and the pasta tasted of nothing. She called her father, who is a chef, and he gave her some advice. He told her to start with three easy recipes and to cook each one several times until she felt confident.

Now Selin can make lentil soup, a vegetable omelette and a chicken salad. She cooks with her flatmates on Sunday evenings and they share the cost of the ingredients. She says that cooking has become a way to relax after a long day of lectures.

title: Unit 4: A Year in Barcelona
content:
Maria moved to Barcelona last September. She has lived there for a year now, and she has already made many friends. At first, she was reluctant to speak Spanish because she was afraid of making mistakes. Her teacher told her that mistakes are a normal part of learning a language.

Every morning, Maria takes the metro to her language school. The school is near the Sagrada Familia, which has been under construction since 1882. She has visited the church three times, but she still wants to see it again when it is finished.

In the evenings, Maria works part-time in a small cafe. She serves coffee and pastries to tourists from all over the world. This job has helped her improve her English as well as her Spanish, because many customers speak English. Last month, a customer from Japan left her a generous tip and a thank-you note.

Maria's biggest challenge has been the Catalan language. Many signs in the city are written in Catalan, and she did not expect this before she arrived. She has started taking an evening Catalan class twice a week. Next summer, she is going to travel to Girona to practise it with local people.

title: Unit 5: The Story of Coffee
content:
According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi. He noticed that his goats became very energetic after they had eaten the red berries of a certain plant. By the fifteenth century, people in Yemen were growing coffee and drinking it to stay awake during long night prayers.

Coffee houses soon became popular in cities such as Istanbul, Cairo and Mecca. People went there not only to drink coffee but also to listen to music, play chess and discuss the news. In the seventeenth century, coffee arrived in Europe, where some people were suspicious of the new drink at first.

Today, coffee is one of the most traded products in the world. Brazil produces more coffee than any other country, and Finland is the country where people drink the most coffee per person. Many people cannot start their day without a cup.

title: Unit 6: Smartphones and Sleep
content:
Many teenagers take their phones to bed and check social media before they go to sleep. Scientists say that this habit can make it harder to fall asleep. The blue light from the screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, so the body produces less of the hormone that makes us sleepy.

A study of two thousand students found that those who used their phones in bed slept about one hour less than those who did not. They also felt more tired during lessons and found it harder to concentrate.

Doctors recommend a few simple changes. Stop using screens at least thirty minutes before bed, and charge your phone outside the bedroom. If you use your phone as an alarm clock, buy a cheap traditional alarm clock instead. Reading a paper book is a good way to relax before sleep.

title: Unit 7: A Weekend in Cappadocia
content:
Last spring, Kerem and his sister spent a long weekend in Cappadocia. They took a night bus from Istanbul, and the journey lasted about eleven hours. They stayed in a small hotel that was built inside a cave, which was cool during the day and warm at night.

On the first morning, they woke up at five o'clock to take a hot air balloon ride. The balloon flew over valleys full of strange rock formations called fairy chimneys. Kerem was a little afraid at first, but the view at sunrise was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen.

In the afternoon, they visited an underground city where people had hidden from enemies thousands of years ago. The tunnels were narrow and dark, and Kerem's sister had to bend down to walk through them. Before they went home, they bought a hand-painted plate from a local pottery workshop.

title: Unit 8: Saving the Sea Turtles
content:
Every summer, sea turtles come to the beaches of southern Turkey to lay their eggs in the sand. After about two months, the baby turtles break out of their eggs at night and walk towards the sea. They find the water by following the light of the moon on the waves.

Unfortunately, bright lights from hotels and restaurants can confuse the baby turtles, and many of them walk in the wrong direction. Plastic rubbish on the beach is another danger, because it can block their path.

Volunteers help to protect the nests. They put small metal cages over the eggs so that people do not step on them, and they ask hotels to turn off their lights at night. Some volunteers are university students who spend their summer holiday on the beach. Thanks to their work, thousands of baby turtles reach the sea safely every year.
